frames.title: Ceremonial Big House Morongo
frames.caption: Ceremonial Big House Morongo, 1800
frames.visitor_caption: A ceremonial Big House on what is today the Morongo Reservation. Long before the town of Beaumont existed, the San Gorgonio Pass was — and remains — the homeland of the Cahuilla and Serrano peoples, with the Big House at the center of ceremonial and community life.
frames.argument: The Ceremonial Big House opens the timeline before the town existed — the Pass as Native homeland, the story's necessary first word.
frames.rationale: The Ceremonial Big House opens the timeline before the town existed — the Pass as Native homeland, the story's necessary first word.
frames.track_label: Track B · Malki Museum + Morongo Tribe consult
frames.source: Malki Museum / Morongo Band (cultural consent required)

frames.title: Weaver
frames.caption: Pauline Weaver, c. 1850s-1860s (Pauline Weaver, d.1867)
frames.visitor_caption: Pauline Weaver — scout, trapper, and one of the earliest non-Native figures to move through the San Gorgonio Pass. His presence bridges the era of Native homeland and the arrival of American settlers.
frames.argument: Pauline Weaver, frontier scout and namesake presence in the Pass — the human bridge between the Native era and Anglo settlement.
frames.rationale: Pauline Weaver, frontier scout and namesake presence in the Pass — the human bridge between the Native era and Anglo settlement.

frames.title: 1860S Stagecoach Downtown Beaumont
frames.caption: Stagecoach downtown Beaumont, 1860
frames.visitor_caption: A stagecoach on Beaumont's dirt main street, around 1860. Before the railroad, the Pass was a stop on the long road west, and the stagecoach was its lifeline to the wider world.
frames.argument: A stagecoach on the dirt main street — Beaumont as a stop on the road west, before the railroad changed everything.
frames.rationale: A stagecoach on the dirt main street — Beaumont as a stop on the road west, before the railroad changed everything.

frames.title: Beaumont Train Depot Calisphere
frames.caption: Beaumont Train Depot, 1875
frames.credit: Beaumont Library District Local History Collection, via Calisphere
frames.visitor_caption: The Beaumont train depot, 1875. The arrival of the Southern Pacific railroad is the hinge of the whole story — the moment a stretch of ranchland became a townsite with a future.
frames.argument: The 1875 depot is the hinge of the whole story: the moment the railroad arrived and the townsite was born. Non-negotiable on the wall.
frames.rationale: The 1875 depot is the hinge of the whole story: the moment the railroad arrived and the townsite was born. Non-negotiable on the wall.

frames.title: Post Office
frames.caption: Post Office at Fifth & Egan Ave., 1890s
frames.visitor_caption: One of Beaumont's earliest post offices. In a young town the post office was among the first institutions of civic life — proof that a scattering of settlers had become a community with a name and an address.
frames.argument: The earliest Post Office view — the founding-era civic seed that the c.1910 stand-in later grew from.
frames.rationale: The earliest Post Office view — the founding-era civic seed that the c.1910 stand-in later grew from.

frames.title: Traditional House On Morongo Reservation
frames.caption: Traditional house on Morongo Reservation, 1900
frames.visitor_caption: A traditional dwelling on the Morongo Reservation, around 1900. As the new town grew nearby, Native life in the Pass continued — a reminder that Beaumont grew up alongside, not in place of, the people who were here first.
frames.argument: A traditional house on the Morongo Reservation, c.1900 — Native life continuing alongside the new town, not erased by it.
frames.rationale: A traditional house on the Morongo Reservation, c.1900 — Native life continuing alongside the new town, not erased by it.
frames.track_label: Track B · Malki Museum + Morongo Tribe consult

frames.title: Clara Stewart Left And Laura May Stewart Right
frames.caption: Clara Stewart, left, and Laura May Stewart, right, c. 1908-1918
frames.visitor_caption: Clara and Laura May Stewart on the family ranch, around 1908. The Stewarts were among the pioneer families who worked the land in Beaumont's early years — and this rare frame keeps the women of the ranch in the picture.
frames.argument: Ranch women in the saddle — the Stewart daughters put Beaumont's pioneer founding families on the wall, and a rare frame of frontier women who ran the land.
frames.rationale: Ranch women in the saddle — the Stewart daughters put Beaumont's pioneer founding families on the wall, and a rare frame of frontier women who ran the land.

frames.title: Morongo Band Of Mission Indians
frames.caption: Morongo Band of Mission Indians, 1908
frames.visitor_caption: Members of the Morongo Band of Mission Indians, 1908. A portrait of the Pass's original community as a living people — central to any honest telling of Beaumont's timeline.
frames.argument: The Morongo Band of Mission Indians, 1908 — a portrait of the Pass's original community as a living people, central to an honest timeline.
frames.rationale: The Morongo Band of Mission Indians, 1908 — a portrait of the Pass's original community as a living people, central to an honest timeline.

frames.title: Beaumont Post Office Ne Corner Fifth St And Egan Ave
frames.caption: Beaumont Post Office NE corner Fifth St. and Egan Ave, c. 1910-1915
frames.visitor_caption: The Beaumont Post Office at Fifth Street and Egan Avenue, about 1910. For decades this corner was the heart of the young town's public life — where residents collected mail, traded news, and crossed paths downtown.
frames.argument: The Post Office at Fifth & Egan anchors the young town's civic core — the corner that was, for decades, the center of Beaumont's public life.
frames.rationale: The Post Office at Fifth & Egan anchors the young town's civic core — the corner that was, for decades, the center of Beaumont's public life.

frames.title: Railroad Workers Luis Estrada Fourth From Right
frames.caption: Railroad workers Luis Estrada fourth from right, c. 1910-1935
frames.visitor_caption: A Southern Pacific railroad crew around 1910, Luis Estrada fourth from the right. The railroad made Beaumont possible, and the Latino laborers who built and kept the line were central to the town's growth.
frames.argument: Railroad crew with Luis Estrada — the Southern Pacific line built Beaumont, and this frame credits the Latino labor that laid and kept the track.
frames.rationale: Railroad crew with Luis Estrada — the Southern Pacific line built Beaumont, and this frame credits the Latino labor that laid and kept the track.

frames.title: Wctu Fountain
frames.caption: WCTU Fountain dedication, Dec. 25, 1910
frames.credit: Leslie A. Rios III Postcard Collection
frames.visitor_caption: The Woman's Christian Temperance Union fountain, 1910. It offered clean water to people and horses alike, and stood as a very public sign that the era's great reform movements reached even a small Pass town.
frames.argument: The WCTU fountain is Beaumont's monument to the temperance movement — proof that national social currents ran straight through a small Pass town.
frames.rationale: The WCTU fountain is Beaumont's monument to the temperance movement — proof that national social currents ran straight through a small Pass town.

frames.title: Wellwood School
frames.caption: Wellwood School, c. 1916–17
frames.visitor_caption: Wellwood School, 1916. As Beaumont grew from scattered ranches into a community, it built schools to raise its own — the mark of families putting down roots.
frames.argument: Wellwood School — the arrival of formal education marks the town's shift from settlement to community raising its own.
frames.rationale: Wellwood School — the arrival of formal education marks the town's shift from settlement to community raising its own.

frames.title: Cherry Festival Queen
frames.caption: Laura May Stewart, first Cherry Festival Queen, 1919
frames.visitor_caption: The Cherry Festival Queen, 1919. Beaumont's orchards made it cherry country, and the annual festival turned the harvest into the town's signature celebration — a tradition that still shapes local identity.
frames.argument: The Cherry Festival Queen crowns Beaumont's identity as cherry country — the orchards were both the economy and the civic celebration.
frames.rationale: The Cherry Festival Queen crowns Beaumont's identity as cherry country — the orchards were both the economy and the civic celebration.

frames.title: George Sumner S And S Store On Fifth Street Interior
frames.caption: George Sumner S and S store on Fifth Street interior, c. 1920s
frames.visitor_caption: Inside George Sumner's S&S Store on Fifth Street in the 1920s. Beyond the civic buildings lay the everyday downtown — the counters where residents actually spent their days and their dollars.
frames.argument: Inside the S&S Store on Fifth Street — Main Street commerce, the daily downtown that a wall of civic buildings alone would miss.
frames.rationale: Inside the S&S Store on Fifth Street — Main Street commerce, the daily downtown that a wall of civic buildings alone would miss.

frames.title: Luis Estrada Family In Their Southern Pacific Railroad Section House Leslie Collection
frames.caption: Luis Estrada family in their Southern Pacific Railroad section house, c. 1940s
frames.visitor_caption: The Estrada family beside their Southern Pacific home in the 1940s. A generation on from the railroad crews, the image shows a family rooted in Beaumont — the human story behind the town's founding industry.
frames.argument: The Estrada family beside their Southern Pacific home — the railroad story carried forward a generation, from labor to a rooted Beaumont family.
frames.rationale: The Estrada family beside their Southern Pacific home — the railroad story carried forward a generation, from labor to a rooted Beaumont family.

frames.title: Beaumont High School
frames.caption: BHS yearbook, 1942
frames.visitor_caption: Beaumont High School, 1942. By mid-century the town's schools had come of age, and generation after generation of residents passed through these halls.
frames.argument: Beaumont High School — education come of age, the institution that a whole mid-century generation of residents passed through.
frames.rationale: Beaumont High School — education come of age, the institution that a whole mid-century generation of residents passed through.

frames.title: First Christian Church Egan Ave Probably Late 1950S A
frames.caption: First Christian Church 701 Egan Ave probably late, 1950
frames.visitor_caption: First Christian Church on Egan Avenue, about 1950. A mainline congregation at the town's civic center — shown alongside Sacred Heart to reflect a Beaumont of many communities worshiping side by side.
frames.argument: First Christian Church on Egan — the mainline civic congregation, paired with Sacred Heart to show a town of two communities worshiping side by side.
frames.rationale: First Christian Church on Egan — the mainline civic congregation, paired with Sacred Heart to show a town of two communities worshiping side by side.

frames.title: Dowling Orchard Fruit Fresh Produce And Dried Fruit Nuts Candy Signs
frames.caption: Dowling Orchard Fruit Fresh Produce and Dried Fruit Nuts Candy signs, c. 1950s-1960s
frames.visitor_caption: The Dowling orchard and packing store in the 1950s. At the fruit industry's height, Beaumont's fresh and dried produce carried the Pass's name far beyond the valley.
frames.argument: The Dowling orchard and packing store at the industry's peak — dried fruit and fresh produce that shipped the Pass's name outward.
frames.rationale: The Dowling orchard and packing store at the industry's peak — dried fruit and fresh produce that shipped the Pass's name outward.

frames.title: Sacred Heart Barrio Church From Leslie Rios
frames.caption: Sacred Heart Barrio Church from, c. late 1950s
frames.credit: Leslie A. Rios III Postcard Collection
frames.visitor_caption: Sacred Heart church in the barrio, late 1940s. A center of faith and gathering for Beaumont's Mexican-American community, it anchored a neighborhood essential to the full story of the town.
frames.argument: Sacred Heart barrio church — the faith and gathering place of Beaumont's Mexican-American community, and one of the few large-format survivors.
frames.rationale: Sacred Heart barrio church — the faith and gathering place of Beaumont's Mexican-American community, and one of the few large-format survivors.

frames.title: Expansion Mansard Roof
frames.caption: Expansion Mansard Roof, 1965
frames.visitor_caption: A new mansard-roofed building marks Beaumont's postwar expansion, 1965. As the mid-century town modernized, it began to outgrow its founding footprint.
frames.argument: The 1960s mansard-roof expansion — postwar Beaumont modernizing, the town outgrowing its founding footprint.
frames.rationale: The 1960s mansard-roof expansion — postwar Beaumont modernizing, the town outgrowing its founding footprint.

frames.caption: Beaumont Developments, 1988
frames.visitor_caption: New development on the edge of Beaumont, 1988. Near the end of the timeline, the town starts its turn toward the growing commuter community it is today.
frames.argument: Late-century development — the timeline's near end, Beaumont becoming the commuter town it is today.
